task: Write one sentence of your own using the word raucous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know raucous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Dawn at the rookery is raucous — ten thousand gulls contesting every ledge at full volume.
Noisy measures decibels and nothing else; raucous adds rowdy, laughing disorder to the volume.
Riotous goes past raucous: the raucous party rattles the windows, while the riotous one has somebody's fence in the bonfire — disorder graduated from sound to deed.

Rowdy is disorderly high spirits — shoving, chanting, spilling over the rails. Raucous needs that unruliness plus the sheer volume of it: a scuffling hallway can be rowdy at a whisper, but a raucous one is heard three classrooms away. Rowdy names the behavior; raucous adds the roar.

Uproarious means convulsed with loud laughter — the comedy club at the night's best punchline. Raucous is broader: loud and unruly in any key, laughing or not. An uproarious room is always laughing; a raucous one may be cheerfully arguing every call with no joke anywhere in it.

Latin raucus crossed into English inside this one adjective and built nothing else here — there is no cousin to spot. If you want a memory hook, listen to the word itself: RAW-kus, a crow's two hoarse syllables.
Raucous means loud and boisterous.

The county fair saves the hog-calling contest for dusk, when the midway is packed: forty contestants bellowing in turn, judges wheezing with laughter, a grandstand of farm families pounding the boards and howling scores nobody asked for.
You could find the event from the parking lot with your eyes shut.
Raucous is not a complaint here — it is the whole point.
Raucous is the exact word because it needs both volume and rowdiness: loud, and loud in an unruly, laughing key.
A jackhammer is merely loud; a library after a prank is merely disorderly.
The raucous grandstand is both at once — noise with jostling life in it, usually more fun to be inside than beside.
Raucous is for noise with rowdy life in it — crowds, gulls, locker rooms, fairs — and it often carries a grin: the raucous reunion was probably a good one.
When the sound is mechanical or joyless, a plainer word like thunderous will serve; raucous insists that somebody is having a loud, unruly time.

Visitors expect the exchange floor to be busy; nothing prepares them for the sound of it.
By the opening bell the pit is raucous — traders bellowing bids over one another, jackets grabbed, tickets flung, the roar carrying two floors up.
A first-timer once asked our guide whether a fight had broken out.
Nothing was wrong, she said; that was just Tuesday.
The din is not chaos for its own sake.
Every shout is an order, every shove a path to a counter-party; the disorder is the market working.
At the closing bell it stops all at once, and the sudden quiet feels louder than anything that came before it.
